senses.gloss: Organized into a clear plan or order.
examples: The class is very *structured* — everything is planned to the minute.
*Structured* interviews ask every candidate the same questions.
He does better with a *more structured* schedule.

position: attributive only — before a noun (*a struggling artist*); after a verb it is the progressive verb, not the adjective

senses.gloss: Having a hard time succeeding or making enough money.
senses.ru: с трудом сводящий концы с концами, бедствующий
examples: He was a *struggling* actor for ten years before he got a part.
The program helps *struggling* readers in third grade.
*Struggling* farmers got some relief from the new law.

position: both — after a verb as two words (*he was strung out*), hyphenated before a noun
contrast: Informal. The two meanings blur, but the drug one is the stronger of the two — be careful about using it lightly.

senses.gloss: Badly affected by a drug you cannot stop taking.
examples: He was *strung out* on painkillers for most of that year.
She looked *strung out* — pale, thin, not sleeping.

senses.gloss: Worn out and on edge from stress or too little sleep.
examples: By finals week everyone is *strung out*.
I'm too *strung out* to make any big decisions right now.
He's even *more strung out* than he was last month.

senses.gloss: Refusing to change your mind, even when you should.
examples: My grandfather is the *most stubborn* man I know.
Don't be so *stubborn* — just let me help you.
She's *stubborn* about doing everything herself.

senses.gloss: Hard to get rid of or deal with, of a thing.
examples: There's a *stubborn* stain on the carpet.
She has a *stubborn* cough that won't go away.

senses.gloss: Short and thick.
examples: He has short, *stubby* fingers.
The dog has a *stubby* little tail.
This pencil is even *stubbier* than the last one.

position: both — usually after a verb: *the window is stuck*
takes: *in* + a place (*stuck in traffic*); *on* + a problem; *with* + something you can't get rid of

senses.gloss: Held fast and unable to move.
examples: The window is *stuck* — I can't get it open.
We were *stuck* in traffic for an hour.

senses.gloss: Unable to go on because you don't know what to do next.
examples: I'm *stuck* on question four.
If you get *stuck*, ask the TA.

senses.gloss: Forced to keep something or someone you don't want.
examples: I got *stuck* with the whole bill.
We're *stuck* with this couch until we can afford a new one.

contrast: Informal, and always about a person who acts superior. Nothing to do with *stuck* meaning 'unable to move'.

senses.gloss: Acting as if you are better than other people.
examples: The other kids thought she was *stuck-up*.
He's not *stuck-up*, he's just shy.
Nobody is *more stuck-up* than that whole crowd.

senses.gloss: Having small metal pieces or jewels set into the surface.
examples: He wore a *studded* leather jacket.
She had on a *studded* belt and heavy boots.

senses.gloss: Dotted all over with something.
examples: The night sky was *studded* with stars.
The cast is *studded* with names you'll recognize.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a studied calm*
contrast: As an adjective it does not mean 'that has been studied'. It means done on purpose while trying to look natural: *studied indifference*.

senses.gloss: Done on purpose and carefully worked out, while meant to look effortless.
examples: He answered with *studied* calm.
Her *studied* indifference fooled nobody.
There was a *studied* casualness about the whole performance.

senses.gloss: Spending a lot of time studying and enjoying it.
examples: She was a quiet, *studious* kid.
He's *more studious* than his brother ever was.
The *studious* ones sat in the front row.

contrast: *Stuffed up* is a different thing: it means your nose is blocked by a cold.

senses.gloss: Filled with something, especially soft filling or food.
examples: The kids sleep with their *stuffed* animals.
We had *stuffed* peppers for dinner.

senses.gloss: So full of food that you can't eat any more.
examples: No more for me — I'm *stuffed*.
Everyone was *stuffed* by the time the pie came out.

senses.gloss: Warm and airless, with no fresh air.
examples: It's *stuffy* in here — can we open a window?
The bedroom gets *stuffier* as the night goes on.

senses.gloss: Formal, old-fashioned and no fun.
examples: It's a *stuffy* old club where you still need a tie.
His parents are nice, just a little *stuffy*.

senses.gloss: Blocked, of your nose.
examples: I have a *stuffy* nose and a sore throat.
My nose gets *stuffy* every spring.

position: both — mostly after a verb; before a noun in *a stunned silence*
contrast: *Stunned* is how the person feels; *stunning* is what causes it. *I was stunned*, but *the news was stunning*.

senses.gloss: So shocked that you can't react.
examples: We were *stunned* by the news.
There was a *stunned* silence in the room.
I was *stunned* that nobody said anything.

contrast: The pair to watch: *stunning* describes the thing (*a stunning view*), *stunned* describes the person (*I was stunned*).

senses.gloss: Extremely beautiful or impressive.
examples: She looked *stunning* in that dress.
The view from the top is *stunning*.
It's the *most stunning* building in the city.

senses.gloss: So surprising that it shocks people.
examples: The team pulled off a *stunning* upset.
It was a *stunning* reversal for the company.

contrast: Nothing to do with the noun *stunt* in *a movie stunt*.

senses.gloss: Kept from growing or developing fully.
examples: The trees along the ridge are *stunted* by the wind.
Poor nutrition leads to *stunted* growth.
His emotional development was *stunted* by those years.

senses.gloss: So shocked, tired or bored that you can barely think.
examples: We sat there *stupefied* by the heat.
He stared at the screen with a *stupefied* look.
The audience was simply *stupefied*.

senses.gloss: Amazingly big or amazingly good.
examples: They did a *stupendous* amount of work in one week.
The final number was *stupendous* — the whole theater stood up.
That's the *most stupendous* thing I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Strongly built and not easily broken.
examples: We need a *sturdy* table for the printer.
These boots are *sturdier* than the ones I had.

senses.gloss: Strong and solid-looking, of a person or animal.
examples: He was a short, *sturdy* man with big hands.
The pony is small but *sturdy*.

senses.gloss: Fashionable and good-looking.
examples: She always looks *stylish*, even in jeans.
It's a small but very *stylish* hotel.
His apartment is the *most stylish* place I've been in.

contrast: *Stylistic* is about style in writing or art; *stylish* is about looking good. A *stylistic* choice is not the same as a *stylish* one.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the style of a piece of writing, music or art.
examples: It's a *stylistic* choice, not a grammar rule.
The two albums have *stylistic* differences but the same band.
The edits were purely *stylistic*.

contrast: American spelling *stylized*; British *stylised*.

senses.gloss: Drawn or done in an artificial style instead of a realistic one.
examples: The logo is a *stylized* bird.
The fight scenes are highly *stylized*.
It's a *stylized* version of a 1950s diner.

contrast: Often a little negative: *suave* suggests charm you don't quite trust. Said SWAHV, not 'soo-AHV'.

senses.gloss: Smooth, confident and polite, usually a man.
examples: He's a *suave* guy in an expensive suit.
The host was *suave* and a little too smooth.
He was the *most suave* person at the party.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *sub-Saharan Africa*

senses.gloss: Of the part of Africa south of the Sahara desert.
examples: Most of the program's work is in *sub-Saharan* Africa.
*Sub-Saharan* countries were hit hardest by the drought.
She studies *sub-Saharan* trade routes.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a subarctic climate*

senses.gloss: Of the cold region just south of the Arctic.
examples: They spent a winter at a *subarctic* research station.
*Subarctic* forests cover much of Canada.
The town has a *subarctic* climate with short summers.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *subatomic particles*

senses.gloss: Smaller than an atom, or happening inside one.
examples: Protons and electrons are *subatomic* particles.
The lab does *subatomic* physics.
At the *subatomic* level the rules are different.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a subconscious fear*
contrast: Also a noun: *your subconscious*. The near-synonym *unconscious* is the one doctors use for someone who has passed out.

senses.gloss: Happening in your mind without you knowing it.
examples: It was a *subconscious* decision — I didn't plan it.
She has a *subconscious* fear of open water.
*Subconscious* bias shows up in who gets called back.

senses.gloss: Quieter and less cheerful than usual.
examples: Everyone was *subdued* after the meeting.
The crowd was strangely *subdued* for a playoff game.

senses.gloss: Soft and not bright, of light or color.
examples: The restaurant has *subdued* lighting.
She painted the walls in *subdued* grays.

position: both — before a noun (*subhuman conditions*) or after a verb
contrast: An ugly word. Calling people *subhuman* is the language of propaganda; *subhuman conditions* is the safer, ordinary use.

senses.gloss: Below what any human being should have to live with, or treated as less than human.
examples: The families lived in *subhuman* conditions.
The camp's *subhuman* conditions shocked the inspectors.
The propaganda painted them as *subhuman*.

position: predicative only — after a verb, always with *to*: *subject to change*
contrast: The adjective is stressed on the first syllable like the noun, SUHB-jikt; the verb *subject* is suhb-JEKT. As an adjective it never stands alone — it always has *to*.

senses.gloss: Likely to be affected by something, or depending on it.
examples: All prices are *subject* to change without notice.
The plan is *subject* to the board's approval.
This area is *subject* to flooding in the spring.

contrast: *Subjective* is based on one person's feelings; *objective* is based on facts anyone can check.

senses.gloss: Based on personal feelings and opinions rather than facts.
examples: Taste in music is completely *subjective*.
That's a *subjective* judgment, not a fact.
Grading essays is *more subjective* than grading math.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the subjunctive mood*
contrast: Also a noun: *use the subjunctive*. In American English you meet it in *I insist that he be there* and *If I were you*.

senses.gloss: Of the verb form used for wishes, demands and unreal situations.
examples: English has a *subjunctive* mood, but it's easy to miss.
*Subjunctive* forms show up after *insist*, *demand* and *suggest*.
The teacher marked it wrong because the *subjunctive* form was missing.

contrast: Also a noun in *from the sublime to the ridiculous*. Said suh-BLYM, not like *subliminal*.

senses.gloss: So beautiful or great that it fills you with wonder.
examples: The view from the ridge was *sublime*.
Her performance was nothing short of *sublime*.
The pie was *sublime* — I had two pieces.

senses.gloss: Affecting your mind below the level where you notice it.
examples: The ad was accused of using *subliminal* messages.
There's a *subliminal* push to buy more than you need.
The effect is *subliminal* — you don't notice it happening.

senses.gloss: Under the surface of the water.
examples: Half the town was *submerged* after the storm.
*Submerged* rocks make the channel dangerous.
The car sat *submerged* in six feet of water.

senses.gloss: Always doing what other people want, without arguing.
examples: He was raised to be quiet and *submissive*.
The dog rolled over in a *submissive* pose.
Her tone got *more submissive* the longer the boss talked.

contrast: The adjective and the noun end in a schwa, suh-BOR-duh-nuht; the verb ends -nate, suh-BOR-duh-nayt.

senses.gloss: Lower in rank or less important than something else.
examples: Everything else is *subordinate* to safety.
She holds a *subordinate* position in the department.

senses.gloss: In grammar, of a clause that depends on a main clause.
examples: *Subordinate* clauses start with words like *because* and *although*.
Underline the *subordinate* clause in each sentence.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *subsequent years*
takes: *to* + noun, in formal writing: *subsequent to the hearing*
contrast: Formal. *Subsequent* just means later; *consequent* means caused by it.

senses.gloss: Coming after something else in time.
examples: The *subsequent* investigation found nothing.
In *subsequent* years the town grew fast.
Each *subsequent* payment is smaller than the last.

senses.gloss: Too willing to obey, or kept in a lower position.
examples: He hated the *subservient* tone his coworkers used with the boss.
The board became *subservient* to the CEO.
She refuses to be *subservient* to anyone.

contrast: Also a common noun: *a subsidiary of the company*.

senses.gloss: Less important than the main thing, and connected to it.
examples: Money was a *subsidiary* concern at that point.
She played a *subsidiary* role in the negotiations.
These questions are *subsidiary* to the main one.

contrast: American spelling *subsidized*; British *subsidised*.

senses.gloss: Paid for in part by a government or an employer, so it costs less.
examples: They live in *subsidized* housing.
The bus passes are *subsidized* by the city.
*Subsidized* school lunches keep a lot of kids fed.

senses.gloss: Below the quality that is required or expected.
examples: The building went up with *substandard* materials.
Tenants complained about *substandard* heating.
The work was *substandard* and had to be redone.

contrast: *Substantial* is about size or solidity; *substantive* is about real content. A *substantial* meal fills you up; a *substantive* discussion gets somewhere.

senses.gloss: Large in amount or important enough to matter.
examples: They made a *substantial* donation to the school.
There's been *substantial* progress since March.

senses.gloss: Solidly built, or big and filling.
examples: We had a *substantial* breakfast before the hike.
The desk is old but *substantial*.

contrast: Not the same as *substantial*: *substantive* changes change the meaning, *substantial* changes are simply big.

senses.gloss: Dealing with the real content of something, not the surface.
examples: The draft needs *substantive* changes, not just edits.
For the first time they had a *substantive* discussion.
Nothing *substantive* came out of the meeting.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a substitute teacher*
contrast: Also a noun (*find a substitute*) and a verb (*substitute butter for oil*). As an adjective it only goes before a noun — you cannot say *the teacher was substitute*.

senses.gloss: Taking the place of the usual person or thing.
examples: We had a *substitute* teacher all week.
The coach put in a *substitute* goalie in the third period.
The district keeps a list of *substitute* drivers.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a subterranean tunnel*

senses.gloss: Under the ground.
examples: The city has a whole *subterranean* network of tunnels.
*Subterranean* rivers run under the limestone.
They found a *subterranean* chamber beneath the church.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a subtropical climate*

senses.gloss: Of the warm regions just outside the tropics.
examples: South Florida has a *subtropical* climate.
*Subtropical* plants won't survive a hard freeze.
The storm formed in *subtropical* waters.

contrast: *Urban* is the city itself, *suburban* the ring of towns around it, *rural* the countryside.

senses.gloss: In or of the suburbs, the residential areas outside a city.
examples: They moved to a *suburban* school district.
*Suburban* traffic is worst around three o'clock.

senses.gloss: Typical of the suburbs — comfortable, ordinary and a little dull.
examples: The whole movie makes fun of *suburban* life.
This street feels *more suburban* than the rest of the city.

contrast: Also a noun for a person: *the government called them subversives*.

senses.gloss: Quietly working against a government, a system or accepted ideas.
examples: The book was banned as *subversive*.
Her comedy is quietly *subversive*.
They were charged with *subversive* activity.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *succeeding generations*
form: -ing from *succeed* in its older sense, to follow
contrast: Here *succeeding* means following, not doing well. *Each succeeding year* means each year after it.

senses.gloss: Coming after, one after another.
examples: Each *succeeding* year the festival got bigger.
*Succeeding* generations told the story differently.
The rule was kept by every *succeeding* administration.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *three successive wins*
contrast: *Successive* means one after another; *successful* means it worked. *Three successive wins* is three in a row.

senses.gloss: Following one after the other without a break.
examples: It rained for five *successive* days.
She won three *successive* elections.
Each *successive* draft got shorter.

senses.gloss: Saying a lot in very few words.
examples: Her answer was *succinct* and clear.
Keep the summary *succinct* — one page at most.
The second draft is *more succinct* than the first.

contrast: Also a noun for plants like aloe and jade: *a shelf of succulents*.

senses.gloss: Juicy and delicious, of meat or fruit.
examples: The lamb was *succulent* and fell off the bone.
We ate *succulent* peaches all through August.

senses.gloss: Thick and fleshy, of a plant that stores water.
examples: Cactus and aloe are *succulent* plants.
*Succulent* leaves hold water through the dry season.

contrast: Like all *-ese* words it adds no *-s* for people: *two Sudanese students*. For one person say *a Sudanese man*, not *a Sudanese*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Sudan, or its people.
examples: The *Sudanese* students meet on Fridays.
Her father is *Sudanese*.
*Sudanese* coffee is served with ginger.

contrast: The adverb is *suddenly*, never *sudden*. *All of a sudden* is a fixed phrase meaning suddenly.

senses.gloss: Happening quickly and without warning.
examples: There was a *sudden* drop in temperature.
A *sudden* noise woke everyone up.
His death was *sudden* — nobody had time to say goodbye.

contrast: More formal than *enough*, and it goes before the noun: *sufficient evidence*, but *enough evidence*.

senses.gloss: As much as is needed.
examples: There wasn't *sufficient* evidence to charge anyone.
One cup of rice is *sufficient* for two people.
The money was *sufficient* to cover the repairs.

senses.gloss: So hot and airless that it is hard to breathe.
examples: The bus was *suffocating* by noon.
A *suffocating* heat hung over the city.

senses.gloss: So controlling that you feel trapped.
examples: She found the relationship *suffocating*.
It was a *suffocating* little town to grow up in.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *Sufi poetry*
contrast: Also a noun for a person: *a Sufi*. The tradition itself is *Sufism*, the mystical side of Islam.

senses.gloss: Of the mystical tradition within Islam.
examples: She teaches *Sufi* poetry in translation.
The *Sufi* orders spread across North Africa.
We heard *Sufi* music at the festival.

senses.gloss: Covered with a layer of sugar.
examples: *Sugar-coated* cereal is basically dessert.
The pills are *sugar-coated* so kids will take them.

senses.gloss: Made to sound nicer than it really is.
examples: He gave us the *sugar-coated* version of the story.
Her report was *sugar-coated*, but the numbers were bad.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *sugarless gum*
contrast: *Sugar-free* is the more common label in American stores; *sugarless* is mostly used for gum and candy.

senses.gloss: Made without sugar.
examples: She chews *sugarless* gum all day.
They sell a *sugarless* version of the syrup.
*Sugarless* candy usually uses sorbitol.

senses.gloss: Containing a lot of sugar, or too sweet.
examples: The kids drink way too many *sugary* sodas.
The sauce was thin and *sugary*.

senses.gloss: Too sweet in the way someone speaks or smiles.
examples: She answered in a *sugary* voice that fooled nobody.
He gave me a *sugary* smile and walked off.

contrast: Watch out for the second meaning: *a suggestive remark* is usually about sex, not about making a suggestion.

senses.gloss: Making you think of something; hinting at it.
examples: The symptoms are *suggestive* of the flu.
The room had a smell *suggestive* of old books.

senses.gloss: Hinting at sex.
examples: The lyrics are pretty *suggestive*.
He made a *suggestive* comment and the table went quiet.

senses.gloss: Wanting to kill yourself.
examples: He called the hotline because he was feeling *suicidal*.
*Suicidal* thoughts are a reason to get help right away.

senses.gloss: So dangerous or foolish that it could destroy you.
examples: Raising prices now would be *suicidal*.
It was a *suicidal* charge across open ground.

position: predicative only — after a verb, with *to* or *for*: *well suited to the job*
comparison: not gradable — but almost always with *well*, *better* or *ideally*: *better suited to the job*
contrast: *Suited* needs *well*, *better* or *ideally* in front of it; plain *He is suited* sounds wrong. *Suitable* is the word that goes before a noun: *a suitable candidate*.

senses.gloss: Right for a particular job, person or situation.
examples: She's well *suited* to this kind of work.
The house isn't *suited* for a family of six.
Of the three, he's the best *suited* to run the meeting.

senses.gloss: Silently angry and showing it, the way a child does.
examples: He's been *sulky* ever since we said no.
She gave me a *sulky* look and went to her room.
The longer we waited, the *sulkier* he got.

contrast: *Sullen* is grown-up and heavy; *sulky* is childish. Neither one is *solemn*, which is serious without the anger.

senses.gloss: Quiet and bad-tempered, refusing to talk.
examples: The boy sat *sullen* and quiet through dinner.
She answered with a *sullen* shrug.

senses.gloss: Dark and gloomy, of the sky or weather.
examples: A *sullen* gray sky hung over the lake.
The morning was cold and *sullen*.

senses.gloss: Hot and humid, of the weather.
examples: It was a *sultry* August afternoon.
August in Houston is *sultrier* than anything I grew up with.

senses.gloss: Attractive in a slow, sexual way.
examples: She has a *sultry* voice.
He gave her a *sultry* look across the bar.

contrast: Also a noun for the people and the language. Not *Sumatran*, which is about the island of Sumatra.

senses.gloss: Of the ancient people of southern Mesopotamia, or their language.
examples: The museum has a room of *Sumerian* tablets.
*Sumerian* is the oldest written language we can still read.
They spent the semester on *Sumerian* myths.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a summa cum laude graduate*
contrast: Latin, 'with highest praise'. It is used even more often as an adverb after *graduate*: *She graduated summa cum laude*. The three levels, lowest first, are *cum laude*, *magna cum laude*, *summa cum laude*.

senses.gloss: Graduating with the highest level of honors.
senses.ru: с высшим отличием, с отличием высшей степени
examples: The program takes mostly *summa cum laude* graduates.
She put her *summa cum laude* honors right at the top of her résumé.
He was the only *summa cum laude* student in his class that year.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *summary judgment*
contrast: Far more common as a noun (*write a summary*). The adjective is legal or official and means done fast, skipping the usual steps: *summary judgment*, *summary dismissal*.

senses.gloss: Done quickly and without the usual procedure.
examples: The judge granted *summary* judgment for the defense.
He was fired in a *summary* dismissal with no hearing.
The report described *summary* executions in the border towns.

contrast: Said exactly like *summary*, but it means 'like summer': *a summery dress*, *summery weather*.

senses.gloss: Like summer, or right for summer.
examples: She wore a light, *summery* dress.
It's unusually *summery* for April.
The menu turns *summery* in June — lots of tomatoes and corn.

senses.gloss: Expensive and grand, in a way that shows.
examples: They served a *sumptuous* dinner.
The hotel lobby is *sumptuous* — marble everywhere.
It was the *most sumptuous* meal I've had in years.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a sun-drenched patio*
contrast: Travel-brochure English. It almost never comes after a verb.

senses.gloss: Getting a lot of bright sunshine.
examples: We ate lunch on a *sun-drenched* patio.
The brochure promised *sun-drenched* beaches.
It's a *sun-drenched* apartment with windows on three sides.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *sun-dried tomatoes*

senses.gloss: Dried in the sun instead of by machine.
examples: Add *sun-dried* tomatoes to the pasta.
They sell *sun-dried* apricots by the pound.
*Sun-dried* bricks are still used in the region.

comparison: not gradable — degree comes from *badly* or *a little*: *badly sunburned*
contrast: American English says *sunburned*; *sunburnt* is mostly British. *Tanned* is the brown you want, *sunburned* is the red you don't.

senses.gloss: Red and sore from too much sun.
examples: My shoulders are *sunburned*.
A *sunburned* tourist came in asking for aloe.
We got back from the lake *sunburned* and happy.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *sundry items*
contrast: Formal or joking, and usually in the phrases *various and sundry* or *all and sundry* (everybody). The noun *sundries* means small odds and ends.

senses.gloss: Of several different kinds, not worth listing one by one.
examples: The drawer is full of pens, cords and *sundry* junk.
She handles billing, scheduling and *sundry* other tasks.
Various and *sundry* relatives showed up for dinner.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a sunken ship*
form: the old participle of *sink*; the modern one is *sunk*
contrast: *Sunken* only goes before a noun. After a verb you need *sunk*: *a sunken ship*, but *the ship has sunk*.

senses.gloss: Lying under the water after sinking.
examples: Divers found the *sunken* ship in 300 feet of water.
They mapped the *sunken* village under the reservoir.

senses.gloss: Hollow, of eyes or cheeks.
examples: He had *sunken* cheeks and dark circles under his eyes.
Her *sunken* eyes made her look exhausted.

senses.gloss: Built lower than the floor or ground around it.
examples: The house has a *sunken* living room.
There's a *sunken* garden behind the church.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a sunlit room*

senses.gloss: Lit by the sun.
examples: We sat in a *sunlit* corner of the café.
The *sunlit* kitchen is the best room in the house.
Dust floated in the *sunlit* air.

senses.gloss: With a lot of sunshine.
examples: It'll be *sunny* and warm all weekend.
They have a *sunny* apartment on the top floor.
Saturday was *sunnier* than Sunday.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and positive.
examples: She has a *sunny* personality.
He keeps a *sunny* outlook even when things go wrong.

position: after the noun — *two eggs sunny-side up*
contrast: Only about fried eggs, and it follows the noun. The usual alternatives in a diner are *over easy*, *over hard* and *scrambled*.

senses.gloss: Fried on one side only, so the yolk stays whole and runny.
examples: I'll have two eggs *sunny-side up*.
He likes his eggs *sunny-side up* with rye toast.
The plate came with hash browns and an egg *sunny-side up*.

contrast: Informal. *Super* is also used in front of other adjectives as an intensifier (*super tired*, *super expensive*) — that is an adverb, not this adjective. In a city apartment building, *the super* is the superintendent.

senses.gloss: Very good indeed.
examples: We had a *super* time at the lake.
That's *super* — thanks for setting it up.
The food was *super*, and the service was fast.

comparison: not gradable — an extreme adjective: *absolutely superb*, not *very superb*

senses.gloss: Excellent — as good as it gets.
examples: The pasta was *superb*.
She gave a *superb* performance.
The seats were *superb* — right behind home plate.

senses.gloss: Fitted with a supercharger for extra engine power.
examples: The truck has a *supercharged* V8.
A *supercharged* engine eats gas.

senses.gloss: Full of energy or strong feeling.
examples: The room was *supercharged* with excitement.
It was a *supercharged* political season.

senses.gloss: Acting as if other people are beneath you.
examples: The waiter had a *supercilious* way of taking orders.
He was polite but faintly *supercilious*.
Nothing ruins a tour like a *supercilious* guide.

senses.gloss: Not deep or careful; only looking at the surface of a subject.
examples: He has a *superficial* knowledge of the subject.
The review was *superficial* — nobody actually read the code.

senses.gloss: Only on the surface, of a wound or damage.
examples: The cuts were *superficial* and healed in a week.
The car had *superficial* damage to the bumper.

senses.gloss: Caring only about looks and appearances, of a person.
examples: She called the whole scene shallow and *superficial*.
He's not *superficial* — he just likes nice clothes.

contrast: The stress is on the second syllable, soo-PUR-floo-uhs, not on the *-flu-*.

senses.gloss: Not needed, because there is already enough.
examples: Half the paragraph is *superfluous* — cut it.
He added a *superfluous* apology at the end.
With the chart right there, the table is *superfluous*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *superhuman strength*

senses.gloss: Greater than any normal person could manage.
examples: It took a *superhuman* effort to finish on time.
The character has *superhuman* strength.
Nobody expects *superhuman* patience, but some would help.

position: both — mostly after a verb, with *on*

senses.gloss: Placed on top of something else so both can be seen.
examples: The subtitles are *superimposed* on the picture.
A grid was *superimposed* over the map.
The *superimposed* images show how far the glacier moved.

contrast: Two jobs, and they feel unrelated: *superlative service* means excellent, while *the superlative form* is the grammar term. Also a noun: *biggest* is a superlative.

senses.gloss: Of the very highest quality.
examples: The staff gave *superlative* service.
It was a *superlative* piece of reporting.

senses.gloss: In grammar, of the form that says 'the most'.
examples: *Biggest* is the *superlative* form of *big*.
Use *the* in front of a *superlative* adjective.

contrast: Also a noun: *the supernatural*.

senses.gloss: Not explainable by the laws of nature — ghosts, magic and the like.
examples: The show is full of *supernatural* stuff — ghosts, curses, the works.
He doesn't believe in anything *supernatural*.
*Supernatural* powers are standard in that genre.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *supersonic flight*

senses.gloss: Faster than the speed of sound.
examples: The Concorde was a *supersonic* jet.
*Supersonic* flight over land is banned in the US.
They tested a *supersonic* missile last spring.

senses.gloss: Believing that certain things bring good or bad luck.
examples: My grandmother was *superstitious* about birds in the house.
Ballplayers are the *most superstitious* people I know.
It's a *superstitious* habit, but I still knock on wood.

comparison: not gradable — degree comes from *closely* or *loosely*: *closely supervised*

senses.gloss: Watched over by someone in charge.
examples: The kids get one hour of *supervised* swimming.
He has *supervised* visits twice a month.
The lab work is closely *supervised*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a supervisory role*

senses.gloss: Having to do with managing other workers.
examples: She moved into a *supervisory* position last year.
The job has no *supervisory* duties.
*Supervisory* staff meet on Mondays.

senses.gloss: Bending easily without cracking, of leather or cloth.
examples: The jacket is old but still *supple*.
The leather gets *more supple* with use.

senses.gloss: Able to bend and move easily, of a body.
examples: Yoga keeps her *supple*.
Dancers stay *supple* into their fifties.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *supplemental income*
contrast: *Supplemental* is the everyday American form — *supplemental insurance*, *Supplemental Security Income*. *Supplementary* means the same thing and sounds more British.

senses.gloss: Added to something to make it complete or bigger.
examples: He drives evenings for *supplemental* income.
The plan comes with *supplemental* dental coverage.
Students got a *supplemental* reading list.

contrast: The same meaning as *supplemental*, which Americans reach for more often. In geometry, *supplementary angles* add up to 180 degrees.

senses.gloss: Added to something else as an extra part.
examples: The packet has *supplementary* materials for teachers.
These notes are *supplementary* to the main text.
*Supplementary* angles add up to 180 degrees.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a supporting role*
contrast: *Supporting* describes the part something plays (*a supporting actor*); *supportive* describes a person who helps you (*a supportive friend*).

senses.gloss: Playing a smaller part next to the main one.
examples: She won an Oscar for Best *Supporting* Actress.
He had a *supporting* role in two movies that year.

senses.gloss: Backing something up — a claim, or a structure.
examples: The lawyer filed *supporting* documents.
Don't cut into a *supporting* wall.

contrast: Not *supporting*: a *supportive* friend helps you, a *supporting* actor has the second-biggest part.

senses.gloss: Giving help, encouragement and sympathy.
examples: Her family has been very *supportive*.
He's *supportive* of the whole idea.
I wish my boss were *more supportive*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the supposed cure*
contrast: Two pronunciations. Before a noun it is suh-POHZD and means 'so-called'. In *be supposed to* it is suh-POHST and means 'ought to': *You're supposed to call first*.

senses.gloss: Said to be so, but probably not true.
examples: The *supposed* cure did nothing at all.
They arrested the *supposed* leader of the group.
His *supposed* alibi fell apart in an hour.

senses.gloss: Held back so it doesn't show, of a feeling or a sound.
examples: She answered with *suppressed* anger.
There was a *suppressed* laugh at the back of the room.

senses.gloss: Kept from being published or made known.
examples: The report was *suppressed* for two years.
*Suppressed* evidence can get a case thrown out.
